methodology.aggregation: mean_per_question; fleet_composite = mean(agent_means); recommendation from composite thresholds

feature.name: Recurring invoice templates
feature.description: Let users save invoice layouts and auto-send on a schedule to repeat clients, with gentle payment reminders.

perQuestion.text: On a scale of 0 to 100, how painful is it today for you to manually create and send repeat invoices to the same clients?
On a scale of 0 to 100, how appealing is the idea of saving reusable invoice templates for recurring clients in LedgerLite?
On a scale of 0 to 100, how important is automatic scheduled sending of recurring invoices to your workflow?
On a scale of 0 to 100, how valuable would automatic, gentle payment reminders be for reducing late payments from repeat clients?
On a scale of 0 to 100, how willing would you be to pay a higher monthly LedgerLite subscription for recurring invoice templates with auto-send and reminders?

executiveSummary: LedgerLite's recurring invoice templates clear the proceed threshold with a fleet composite mean of 73.9, median 75.5, and 75% likely to adopt. The strongest signals are template appeal (mean 85.6, with 93 agents rating 80-100), gentle payment reminder value (mean 81), and automatic scheduled sending importance (mean 74.7), while today's recurring invoice pain is substantial (mean 69.3). Omar, the solo consultant segment, leads adoption propensity (count 25, compositeMean 81.7), followed by Maya (25, 75.9), Priya (25, 74.4), and Jordan (25, 63.7). The central caveat is monetization: willingness to pay has a mean of 59 and no ratings in 80-100, and the panel themes show price sensitivity plus a strong preference for modest add-on or bundled pricing. The feature should proceed, but with a modest or bundled price path, optional review-before-send controls, and reliable setup/exports/integrations.
strengths: Template reuse is the standout: recurring invoice template appeal mean 85.6 (median 86; 93 of 100 responses 80-100), supported by positive themes around reusable templates saving recurring billing time (approx 48) and removing copy-paste (approx 50).

Gentle reminders address an emotional and operational pain: gentle payment reminder value mean 81 (median 82; 67 responses 80-100), with positive themes on reducing late-payment chasing (approx 46) and gentle reminders for late payments (approx 49).

Auto-send is important enough to matter: auto-send schedule importance mean 74.7 (median 76; 45 responses 80-100), with positive theme auto-send and scheduled sending (approx 43), though it is strongest when paired with control.

The underlying manual pain is real for core repeat-billing users: recurring invoice pain severity mean 69.3 (median 72; 80 of 100 responses 60-100), and positive themes include time savings across multiple retainer clients (approx 25) and mobile invoicing between client calls (approx 25).

There is a professionalization benefit for newer users and a self-serve adoption path: positive themes include professional-looking invoices for new freelancers (approx 25) and quick self-serve setup without steep learning curve (approx 14).
blockers: Willingness to pay is the clearest constraint: mean 59, median 59, IQR 54-65, with 0 responses in 80-100 and 47 in 40-59. Themes show negative price sensitivity (approx 50) and mixed preference for modest add-on or bundling (approx 50).

Auto-send can trigger control concerns: mixed theme auto-send needs optional review/control approx 42, plus review-before-send and per-client control approx 12. Panel language emphasizes variable line items, client-name risk, and audit trails, so hands-off automation should not be the only mode.

Reliability, setup, and integrations are adoption gates for some: mixed themes quick setup, mobile reliability, integrations approx 21, and clean exports/reliable integrations approx 17. Exports and integration reliability are especially important for bookkeeping workflows.

Urgency is uneven across the market: mixed theme limited repeat clients reduce urgency approx 18, and the Jordan new freelancer segment shows recurrent pain at only 47.2 and auto-send importance at 59.5. New freelancers may value templates and reminders but not scheduled auto-send or a paid upgrade yet.
segmentInsights: Omar — solo consultant (count 25, compositeMean 81.7): highest adoption propensity. Pain 83.2, template appeal 89.6, auto-send importance 86.7, reminder value 80.0, WTP 68.8. The panel links this to retainer billing copy-paste and cash-flow improvement, but even this segment conditions adoption on a reasonable add-on cost.

Maya — freelance designer (count 25, compositeMean 75.9): strong fit. Template appeal 86.7 and reminder value 83.8, with pain 72.4, auto-send 77.0, and WTP 59.4. Mobile use between client calls and review-before-send for variable invoices are recurring qualifiers; price must stay a small add-on or bundled.

Priya — part-time bookkeeper (count 25, compositeMean 74.4): solid but operationally cautious. Pain 74.4, template appeal 85.3, auto-send 75.8, reminder value 80.1, WTP 56.6. Reminders and export-friendly records are valuable, while auto-send needs auditability and modest cost.

Jordan — new freelancer (count 25, compositeMean 63.7): weakest current fit. Template appeal 80.6 and reminder value 80.0 are healthy, but pain 47.2, auto-send 59.5, and WTP 51.1 show limited repeat-client urgency. The near-term appeal is professional-looking templates and gentle reminders, not fully automated recurring billing.
dataLimitations: Synthetic panel of 100 agents; all 100 completed with 0 missing, but results are simulated directional judgments rather than observed adoption, payment, or retention behavior.

Segments are archetype-based with fixed counts of 25 each, not a probability sample of independent professionals and micro-businesses in North America and Western Europe; geographic and firmographic splits are not provided.
Willingness to pay is self-reported, compressed (mean 59, IQR 54-65, no 80-100), and likely sensitive to packaging; it should not be treated as precise price elasticity.

Themes and representative quotes are approximate and qualitative; they explain direction but do not prove causality or quantify feature-level conversion. Implementation details for setup, mobile reliability, exports, integrations, and review controls could materially change real-world results.
